title: Country captain
subtitle: Anglo-Indian curried chicken stew
excerpt: A mild, aromatic chicken stew of Anglo-Indian origin: chicken braised with onion, tomatoes, curry powder, and raisins, finished with toasted almonds. A bridge dish between British and Indian cooking, popular in the colonial era.
sourceNotes: Country Captain appears in British and American colonial-era cookery books from at least the 1840s. The dish travelled between India, Britain, and the American South via sea captains, which may be the origin of the name. Cross-referenced with Madhur Jaffrey, An Invitation to Indian Cooking (1973) and the Colonial Williamsburg cookbook traditions.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes for up to 3 months. Thaw and reheat gently.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Improves with a day's resting.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make a day ahead; the flavour deepens overnight.

content.text: Country captain is a mild, slightly sweet curried chicken dish. The combination of curry powder (British-style mild blend), raisins, and almonds reads as distinctly Anglo-Indian: it is not a dish you would find in a contemporary Indian restaurant, but it is flavourful in its own right and makes excellent weeknight food. Serve over plain boiled rice.

items.prepNote: skin on, or 4 bone-in chicken pieces
one tin of chopped tomatoes, or 4 fresh ripe

content.text: Season the chicken pieces with salt. Heat the oil in a large casserole over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken pieces skin side down for 4 to 5 minutes until golden. Flip and brown the other side. Remove and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Cook the onion and green pepper in the same pot for 8 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and curry powder and cook for 2 minutes, stirring.
Add the tomatoes and stock. Stir well, scraping any browned bits from the base. Return the chicken pieces to the pot, skin side up. Add the raisins.
Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cook, partially covered, for 35 to 40 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce has reduced and thickened. Season.
Serve over boiled basmati rice. Scatter with toasted almonds and chopped parsley.

items.cause: Too much liquid or not reduced enough
items.fix: Remove the lid for the last 15 minutes to concentrate the sauce.
Use medium curry powder or add a pinch of cayenne at the end.

items.cause: Added too early and cooked too long
items.fix: Add the raisins only for the last 15 minutes of cooking so they retain some texture.
For the last 10 minutes, remove the lid. The skin won't be crisp but it should not be wet and soft.

content.text: Country captain is a peripatetic dish that crossed the Indian Ocean in both directions. It appears in Indian-British colonial households from the early 19th century, in American cookbooks from the 1850s (where it became associated with the American South, particularly Georgia), and in various forms across the cuisines of the former British Empire. It is a bridge dish: distinctly curried but mild enough to have been adopted by British and American home cooks who might otherwise avoid Indian spicing. It deserves a wider audience today.
